paper_claims.claim: The original MAX anomaly's value-weighted abnormal returns are explained by mispricing/behavioral factor models (SY, DHS) and equity issuance: MAX's predictive power is a manifestation of persistent mispricing, not lottery preference.
MAX^beta (beta-neutralized MAX) earns a significant value-weighted long-short abnormal return robust to all standard risk AND mispricing factor models, driven by both legs - a new, distinct anomaly.

The MAX^beta spread's source shifts across investor clienteles: retail investors overpay for high-MAX^beta stocks (low-INST tier), while institutions earn a premium holding low-MAX^beta stocks (high-INST tier) - heterogeneous skewness preferences.
The low-MAX^beta premium is durable - earned every month over a two-year holding horizon - whereas the MAX effect corrects within 1-2 months; equilibrium compensation, not mispricing.

The MAX^beta 10-1 alpha spread is approximately invariant across aggregate equity-issuance regimes (and stays significant in low-sentiment states), while the MAX spread concentrates in high-sentiment and high-issuance states.

tables.description: VW one-month-ahead excess returns and alphas (CAPM, FF3, FFC4, FFCPS, FF5, FF6, FF6PS, SY, DHS) for MAX deciles
tables.replication_meaning: Demonstrates the benchmark MAX univariate sort: MAX constructed as mean of 5 highest daily returns, monthly decile sorts on the CRSP universe (shrcd 10/11, price>=5, SIC exclusions, >=15 daily obs), VW weighting, RF subtraction, and all nine factor-model alpha regressions with Newey-West 6-lag t-stats. Headline claim C1 (MAX spreads explained by SY/DHS mispricing models) depends on this construction being correct.
tables.paper_quote: This table reports the performance of decile portfolios constructed monthly by sorting stocks based on MAX, defined as the average of the five highest daily returns within a month. Portfolio 1 contains stocks with the lowest MAX, while Portfolio 10 contains stocks with the highest MAX. The reported values are value-weighted average one-month-ahead excess returns (RET – RF), as well as alphas from risk-adjusted models (CAPM, FF3, FFC4, FFCPS, FF5, FF6, and FF6PS) and mispricing-adjusted models (SY and DHS). (L970-972)

tables.description: Fama-MacBeth regressions of one-month-ahead excess returns on MAX and controls (MIS, CE, BETA, SIZE, BM, REV, MOM, ILLIQ, ROE, I/A, IVOL)
tables.replication_meaning: Demonstrates the firm-level Fama-MacBeth methodology for the MAX side: fixed sample (all 12 independent variables non-missing), monthly cross-sectional regressions, time-series average of slopes, NW 6-lag t-stats, and the cross-sectional 1%/99% winsorization applied monthly on the fixed sample. Validates the control-variable constructions (SIZE, BM, REV, MOM, ILLIQ, ROE, I/A, IVOL, MIS, CE) that claim C1 depends on.
tables.paper_quote: This table reports the results of firm-level Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions of one-month-ahead excess stock returns on MAX and a set of control variables. (L1717)

tables.description: VW one-month-ahead excess returns and alphas (CAPM, FF3, FFC4, FFCPS, FF5, FF6, FF6PS, SY, DHS) for MAX^beta deciles (beta deciles then MAX deciles within)
tables.replication_meaning: Demonstrates the headline MAX^beta double-sort construction: monthly decile sort on 252-day market beta, then MAX deciles within each beta decile, regrouping by MAX rank across beta deciles, VW returns, and all nine factor models. Headline claim C2 (MAX^beta spread robust to risk AND mispricing models, driven by both legs) depends on this construction being correct.
tables.paper_quote: The portfolios are constructed using a conditional sorting procedure. First, stocks are sorted into decile portfolios based on their market beta. Then, within each beta-sorted portfolio, stocks are further sorted into decile portfolios based on their MAX (defined as the average of the five highest daily returns within a month). To form the final deciles, we group together all stocks with the same MAX ranking, n, across the different beta portfolios. (L2055)

tables.description: Durability of MAX and MAX^beta premia: calendar-time FF6PS alphas by holding horizon K (1-24 months), strategies and legs
tables.replication_meaning: Demonstrates the Jegadeesh-Titman (1993) calendar-time overlapping-portfolio methodology: K cohorts held without rebalancing, 1/K weights, single monthly series per horizon, FF6PS alpha with fixed 6-lag Newey-West, CR(K)=K*alpha_K. Claim C4 (low-MAX^beta premium durable over 2 years vs MAX correcting in 1-2 months) depends on this methodology.
tables.paper_quote: For each horizon K we form the strategy every month, hold each cohort for K months without rebalancing, and in each calendar month average the K most recently formed cohorts with weight 1/K each, yielding a single monthly return series (Jegadeesh and Titman, 1993; Fama, 1998). (L2997)
